questions.statement: Choose the option that corrects the error: 'She has lived in this town since five years.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests grammar, vocabulary, reading and writing under the same conditions as the real session.

options.text: She has lived in this town for five years.
options.feedback: Correct! 'For' is followed by a period of time, and 'since' is followed by a point in time.

options.text: She has lived in this town during five years.
options.feedback: 'During' is used for an event or a specific period, not for a duration of living.

options.text: She is living in this town since five years.
options.feedback: 'Is living' is the present continuous and does not combine with 'since' plus a length of time.

options.text: She lives in this town since five years.
options.feedback: 'Lives' is the simple present, which cannot be used with 'since' plus a duration.

questions.explanation:
'For' and 'since' are not interchangeable. The choice depends on whether the phrase names a length or a starting point.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the option with the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They will build a new library next year.'
questions.context: A mock examination includes transformation items in which the tense must be preserved.

options.text: A new library will build next year.
options.feedback: 'Will build' is active and keeps the agent in the subject position.

options.text: A new library will be built next year.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Will be built' is the future passive, formed with 'will be' plus the past participle.

options.text: A new library is built next year.
options.feedback: 'Is built' is the present passive, and the event is placed in the future.

options.text: A new library was built next year.
options.feedback: 'Was built' is the past passive, and the event has not happened yet.

questions.explanation:
When a sentence is put into the passive, the tense of the auxiliary is kept and only the order of the elements changes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'If I ____ more time, I would take a course in graphic design.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests the conditionals with an unreal situation in the present.

options.text: have
options.feedback: 'Have' would form the first conditional, which describes a real possibility.

options.text: will have
options.feedback: 'Will have' is not used in the if-clause of any conditional.

options.text: had
options.feedback: Correct! The second conditional uses the past simple of 'have' in the if-clause.

options.text: would have
options.feedback: 'Would have' inverts the usual order of the third conditional.

questions.explanation:
Each conditional has its own fixed pair of tenses. Choosing the wrong one changes the type of situation being described.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which word best completes the sentence: 'The report was written ____ the committee and approved by the board.'
questions.context: A mock examination includes items that test prepositions in technical registers.

options.text: of
options.feedback: 'Of' expresses possession and never names an agent in the passive.

options.text: from
options.feedback: 'From' expresses origin, not responsibility for the action.

options.text: with
options.feedback: 'With' names the instrument used, not the person who acted.

options.text: by
options.feedback: Correct! In the passive, 'by' names the agent that performed the action.

questions.explanation:
'By' is the agent preposition of the passive, and no other preposition can replace it in that role.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the option that best completes: 'She is the only student who ____ the exam twice.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests the agreement of subject and verb inside a relative clause.

options.text: has taken
options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect is used for a past action with present relevance in a clause of this kind.

options.text: have taken
options.feedback: 'Have taken' does not agree with the singular subject 'the only student'.

options.text: had taken
options.feedback: 'Had taken' is the past perfect, which would refer to an earlier past than the one described.

options.text: taking
options.feedback: 'Taking' is a participle and cannot be the verb of a relative clause without an auxiliary.

questions.explanation:
The verb of the relative clause agrees with the antecedent 'the only student', and the tense carries the meaning of the sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the word that best fits: 'The results were ____; the experiment must be repeated.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests the ability to deduce the right word from the context of a statement.

options.text: conclusive
options.feedback: 'Conclusive' is the opposite of what the sentence states.

options.text: inconclusive
options.feedback: Correct! 'Inconclusive' describes results that do not settle the question, which is what the repetition implies.

options.text: concluding
options.feedback: 'Concluding' is a participle and cannot describe results in this position.

options.text: conclude
options.feedback: 'Conclude' is a verb and cannot be used as an adjective before the noun.

questions.explanation:
A good gap-fill answer is chosen for its meaning in the sentence, and the reason clause is the strongest clue available.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the word 'although' correctly?
questions.context: A mock examination tests conjunctions and the structures that follow them.

options.text: Although it was raining until the match continued.
options.feedback: The first sentence attaches a second clause to 'although' without a second contrast.

options.text: Although of the rain, the match continued.
options.feedback: 'Although of' adds a preposition that does not belong after the conjunction.

options.text: Although it was raining, the match continued.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Although' is followed by a clause with a subject and a verb, and it introduces a contrast.

options.text: Although the rain, the match continued.
options.feedback: 'Although' cannot be followed directly by a noun phrase in this construction.

questions.explanation:
'Although' takes a clause and creates a contrast with the main clause. 'Despite' is the form that takes a noun phrase.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the passage: 'The library opens at seven. Students may borrow up to four books for two weeks.' What is the main fact?
questions.context: A mock examination includes short reading passages followed by questions about their content.

options.text: The number of students in the school.
options.feedback: The number of students is not mentioned.

options.text: The history of the library building.
options.feedback: The history of the building is not mentioned at all.

options.text: The cost of the books.
options.feedback: The cost of the books is not mentioned.

options.text: The borrowing conditions of the library.
options.feedback: Correct! The passage states the opening hour and the borrowing limit, which together are the borrowing conditions.

questions.explanation:
The main fact is what the whole passage is about. A detail that is not mentioned cannot be the main fact.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the passage: 'Sales fell for three months and then recovered.' What can be inferred?
questions.context: A mock examination tests inference from a short passage rather than retrieval of a stated fact.

options.text: The fall was temporary.
options.feedback: Correct! A recovery after a fall shows that the fall was not permanent.

options.text: The fall was permanent.
options.feedback: 'Permanent' is the opposite of what the recovery indicates.

options.text: Sales rose during the same three months.
options.feedback: The passage says sales fell, not that they rose.

options.text: The company closed the branch.
options.feedback: Nothing in the passage mentions a branch or a closure.

questions.explanation:
An inference combines two facts in the passage. The recovery after the fall is what licenses the conclusion about duration.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best begins a formal letter of complaint?
questions.context: A mock examination includes a writing task that requires a formal register.

options.text: Your service is bad.
options.feedback: The first sentence is a bare judgement with no politeness and no context.

options.text: I am writing to report a problem with the service in your restaurant.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence states the purpose of the letter formally and names what the complaint concerns.

options.text: I want to complain about the food, which was not good.
options.feedback: The third sentence is a request rather than a formal statement of purpose.

options.text: Hey, the food was awful last night, ok?
options.feedback: The fourth sentence is spoken register and would not appear in a formal letter.

questions.explanation:
The first sentence of a formal letter declares its purpose, and the register has to be consistent from the first line.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the option that correctly uses a modal of deduction: 'The lights are off, so everyone ____ already gone home.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests the modal system as a whole.

options.text: must to have
options.feedback: 'Must to have' adds an infinitive marker that modals never take.

options.text: must having
options.feedback: 'Must having' places a gerund after a modal, which is not a possible form.

options.text: must have
options.feedback: Correct! 'Must have' plus a participle draws a certain conclusion about a past action.

options.text: must be have
options.feedback: 'Must be have' uses two auxiliaries in a way that English does not allow.

questions.explanation:
A modal never changes form, so all the extra elements in the distractors break the structure that the modal requires.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses a relative pronoun correctly after a preposition?
questions.context: A mock examination tests the forms of relative pronouns in formal written English.

options.text: The person to who I spoke was very helpful.
options.feedback: 'To who' uses the object form after a preposition, which is not the standard usage.

options.text: The person to which I spoke was very helpful.
options.feedback: 'To which' would be used for things, and the person here is a human being.

options.text: The person to what I spoke was very helpful.
options.feedback: 'To what' cannot function as a relative pronoun after a preposition.

options.text: The person to whom I spoke was very helpful.
options.feedback: Correct! After a preposition, the relative pronoun takes its subject form, which is 'whom' for people.

questions.explanation:
After a preposition the relative pronoun is in its subject form, and the form for people is 'whom' rather than 'who'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct word order: 'Rarely ____ such a large crowd at a school event.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests inversion with fronted negative adverbs.

options.text: have I seen
options.feedback: Correct! The fronted negative adverb 'rarely' requires the auxiliary before the subject.

options.text: I have seen
options.feedback: 'I have seen' keeps the declarative order, which is not possible with a fronted negative.

options.text: I saw
options.feedback: 'I saw' keeps the order and also changes the tense unnecessarily.

options.text: saw I
options.feedback: 'Saw I' inverts the main verb and the subject and leaves out the auxiliary the construction needs.

questions.explanation:
A fronted negative adverb moves the auxiliary in front of the subject, and the rest of the clause keeps its normal order.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option is the best synonym for 'reluctant' in a formal text?
questions.context: A mock examination tests vocabulary in context rather than simple definition matching.

options.text: eager
options.feedback: 'Eager' is the opposite of the original meaning.

options.text: unwilling
options.feedback: Correct! 'Unwilling' carries the same meaning as 'reluctant' and fits the register of a formal text.

options.text: certain
options.feedback: 'Certain' is unrelated to willingness in any sense.

options.text: pleased
options.feedback: 'Pleased' is also the opposite of the original meaning.

questions.explanation:
A synonym must preserve the meaning, not merely belong to the same part of speech. Three of these options reverse the meaning.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence contains a verb tense error?
questions.context: A mock examination asks the student to find the sentence in which the sequence of tenses is broken.

options.text: By the time we reached the hall, the film had already started.
options.feedback: The first sentence uses the past perfect correctly for the earlier event.

options.text: By the time we reach the hall, the film starts.
options.feedback: The second sentence uses the present simple and the present simple consistently, so it is coherent.

options.text: By the time we reached the hall, the film has already started.
options.feedback: Correct! This sentence mixes the past perfect with a present perfect for the earlier of two past events.

options.text: By the time we reached the hall, the film starts.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence is inconsistent in the same way, since the two clauses do not share a time frame.

questions.explanation:
Two past events need a sequence: the earlier one in the past perfect. The present perfect belongs to a different relation with the present.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the passage: 'The factory closed in 2011. Since then, the river has become much cleaner.' What is the relation between the two sentences?
questions.context: A mock examination tests the logical relations between the sentences of a short passage.

options.text: The second sentence contradicts the first.
options.feedback: Claiming a contradiction reverses the relation: the later sentence actually supports what came before it.

options.text: The two sentences describe the same year.
options.feedback: A factory closed in one year cannot be about the same year as a change that followed it, so this reading is wrong.

options.text: The first sentence is the consequence of the second.
options.feedback: Cause and effect cannot be reversed here: the earlier sentence is the starting point, not the outcome.

options.text: The second sentence describes a change that began after the event in the first.
options.feedback: Correct! The phrase 'since then' links a present state to a starting point named earlier in the passage.

questions.explanation:
A connective of time states a relation between two facts. Reading it correctly is what tells the reader which event came first.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is appropriate as a concluding sentence of an argument?
questions.context: A mock examination includes a task in which the candidate must close an argument.

options.text: For these reasons, the proposal deserves serious consideration.
options.feedback: Correct! The sentence gathers the reasons and restates the position the argument supports.

options.text: The proposal is a proposal.
options.feedback: The second sentence repeats a word and says nothing.

options.text: Some people like proposals and some do not.
options.feedback: The third sentence reports a division of opinion without choosing one.

options.text: Proposals are usually discussed in meetings.
options.feedback: The fourth sentence introduces a general fact that closes no argument.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion must refer to the reasons already given and restate the position the writer defends.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrasal verb means to discover something unexpected?
questions.context: A mock examination tests the meaning of phrasal verbs as vocabulary items.

options.text: find in
options.feedback: 'Find in' is not a complete phrasal verb in this sense.

options.text: find out
options.feedback: Correct! 'Find out' means to discover a fact that was not known before.

options.text: find up
options.feedback: 'Find up' would mean to search for something higher, and it is not standard usage here.

options.text: find about
options.feedback: 'Find about' is not an expression of the English language.

questions.explanation:
Particles carry a fixed meaning in a phrasal verb, and three of these combinations are not part of the language.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct sentence: 'There is not ____ students in the library yesterday.'
questions.context: A mock examination tests agreement of the verb and the quantifier with the subject.

options.text: There is not many students in the library yesterday.
options.feedback: 'Is not' is the present, which contradicts 'yesterday'.

options.text: There was not many students in the library yesterday.
options.feedback: 'Was not' does not agree with the plural subject 'students'.

options.text: There were not many students in the library yesterday.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were not' matches the past time expression, and 'many' is the quantifier used with a countable plural noun.

options.text: There are not much students in the library yesterday.
options.feedback: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns, and 'are' does not agree with the past time expression.

questions.explanation:
The verb follows the subject and the time expression, and the quantifier follows the countability of the noun. Two independent agreements are tested in one sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option expresses an opinion most appropriately in an academic essay?
questions.context: A mock examination tests whether a candidate can express an opinion in the register the task requires.

options.text: The policy is rubbish.
options.feedback: 'Rubbish' is a spoken insult and does not belong in a formal essay.

options.text: Everyone knows the policy is bad.
options.feedback: 'Everyone knows' claims universal agreement without evidence.

options.text: The policy is obviously wrong.
options.feedback: 'Obviously wrong' is an absolute judgement that the essay cannot support.

options.text: It could be argued that the policy needs revision.
options.feedback: Correct! 'It could be argued that' presents a position as defensible, which is the academic way to state an opinion.

questions.explanation:
Academic style qualifies claims. An opinion presented without qualification is marked down even when it is the right opinion.
---
questions.subject: ingles
